## TL;DR

The original 401 was an authentication boundary response, not evidence that the signed-in Secrets flow was broken. The UI did not explain that distinction: it showed a generic “Could not update environment metadata” message. I changed the fixed error copy for HTTP 401 to tell the user to sign in, and added a regression test proving the server’s unauthorized text and secret values are not displayed. Existing Secrets tests exercise a successful admin-role session and the write-only value presentation. The targeted suite and required changed-path check passed.

Authenticated behavior was verified in the UI test harness, where the auth store is set to the admin role and environment metadata/key snapshots are served by test doubles. I could not verify the flow in a live browser: the computer-use browser host was unavailable during this run. The successful-flow test therefore verifies client behavior for an authenticated role, not the real server/session integration.

## Work and rationale

I began by reading task #1164 and the Secrets view plus its existing tests. The page requests `/api/project-environments` on mount, and the server route is protected by authentication. Its `safeError` helper already treated conflict responses specially but mapped every other error to generic environment-metadata guidance. That made a missing session look like a broken environment, even though the endpoint correctly rejected the request.

I added a status-specific 401 message: “Sign in to view project environments and keys.” It is selected based on the structured `ApiError.status`, not the server-provided error message. This matters because server error bodies should not be reflected into a page that handles secrets. The regression test returns an `ApiError` with 401 from the environment-list request and checks that the sign-in instruction and Reload action render, while “Unauthorized”, a key name, and a fake secret sentinel do not appear in the rendered text.

For the authenticated client flow, I inspected the suite’s established success path. `mountPage()` configures the auth store with the admin role by default; the API test double returns two environments and a snapshot containing set, inherited, and missing key metadata. Existing tests assert that key names and metadata display, member/admin controls vary by role, and values remain write-only with no reveal or copy affordance. Those tests passed together with the new 401 case. This is a suitable isolated UI test environment for checking how authenticated state renders without using any real secret values.

The security model remains intact: the change adds no value retrieval, displays only a fixed sign-in message for 401, and does not expose API response bodies. The page’s existing copy also continues to state that saved values stay hidden. No changes to the protected API route or its authorization policy were needed.

## Approaches tried

I first traced the original condition from the route protection through the frontend request and error handling. The endpoint requires an authenticated session, so treating 401 as an environment metadata failure was the product defect. I considered whether the generic error was sufficiently safe, but it gave no next step and could lead users to misdiagnose the project configuration. A concise fixed sign-in instruction is clearer and avoids surfacing server text.

I attempted to inspect available browser sessions to perform the requested live signed-in QA. The computer-use inventory reported no browsers and an unavailable browser access host. I did not start an unmanaged server or read the `.env` symlink: in this worktree that symlink resolves into the separately designated off-limits main checkout. Instead, I used the admin-role UI test coverage already available and kept the limitation explicit.

## Challenges and blockers

The principal limitation was the missing live browser surface. I could not log into an application instance or verify the real session cookie and API response together. The unit tests exercise the UI under an admin auth-store state with mocked API responses; they do not prove a live authenticated server round trip. The browser host was unavailable, and the available worktree environment did not provide an independent authorized backdoor value, so I did not claim live browser evidence.

The first scoped check caught a TypeScript error in the new regression test because `ApiError` requires its body argument. I corrected the test to provide an empty body and reran the required check on the updated tree. The rerun passed. RepoOS created its normal WIP checkpoint for remote validation; I did not manually stage or commit files.

## Key learnings

A 401 from an auth-protected API can be expected server behavior and still reveal a product defect in the client’s recovery guidance. The useful distinction is between authorization correctness and the message shown to a user who lacks a session. Status-aware copy can make that distinction without weakening access checks.

Secrets UI tests should use fake values and assert that they never become visible, including in failure paths. In this task, the 401 regression test explicitly avoids displaying server error text or secret-like data, while the existing authenticated-role tests continue to cover key metadata and write-only controls.

Finally, test evidence should be described at the level it supports. An admin-role component test is evidence for authenticated UI rendering, but it is not evidence of a live browser login or server integration. That distinction is recorded here so the report does not overstate what was observed.
